questions.prompt: Verify that \(y=Ce^{2x}\) solves \(dy/dx=2y\), where \(C\) is a constant.
questions.answer: Differentiate the proposed solution: \(dy/dx=2Ce^{2x}\). Since \(y=Ce^{2x}\), the right-hand side of the equation is \(2y=2Ce^{2x}\). The derivative equals the right-hand side, so \(y=Ce^{2x}\) solves \(dy/dx=2y\).

The differential equation gives the derivative of \(y\). Integrate both sides with respect to \(x\): \(y=\int 3x^2\,dx\). This gives \(y=x^3+C\), where \(C\) is an arbitrary constant. Therefore the general solution is \(y=x^3+C\).
Integrate the differential equation: \(y=\int 2x\,dx=x^2+C\). Use the initial condition \(y(0)=5\): \(5=0^2+C\), so \(C=5\). Therefore the solution is \(y=x^2+5\).

Separate the variables: \(\frac{1}{y}\,dy=x\,dx\), assuming \(y\ne0\). Integrate both sides: \(\ln|y|=x^2/2+C\). Exponentiating gives \(|y|=e^C e^{x^2/2}\), so \(y=Ae^{x^2/2}\). The zero solution is included by \(A=0\), so the general solution is \(y=Ae^{x^2/2}\).
Rewrite the equation as \(dy/dx=-y\). Separate variables: \(\frac{1}{y}\,dy=-dx\). Integrate to get \(\ln|y|=-x+C\). Exponentiating gives \(y=Ce^{-x}\), including the zero solution when \(C=0\).

This is linear with integrating factor \(\mu(x)=e^{\int2\,dx}=e^{2x}\). Multiplying by \(e^{2x}\) gives \(e^{2x}y'+2e^{2x}y=6e^{2x}\), so \((e^{2x}y)'=6e^{2x}\). Integrate: \(e^{2x}y=3e^{2x}+C\). Divide by \(e^{2x}\) to get \(y=3+Ce^{-2x}\).

questions.prompt: Solve \(dy/dx=x+y\) is not separable by simple algebra. State whether it is linear and identify \(P(x)\) and \(Q(x)\) in \(y'+P(x)y=Q(x)\).
questions.answer: Move the \(y\) term to the left: \(y'-y=x\). This matches \(y'+P(x)y=Q(x)\). Comparing terms gives \(P(x)=-1\) and \(Q(x)=x\). Therefore the equation is first-order linear, even though it is not directly separable in the form \(g(y)y'=h(x)\).
Separate variables: \(\frac{1}{y}\,dy=4\,dx\). Integrate: \(\ln|y|=4x+C\), so \(y=Ae^{4x}\). Apply \(y(0)=2\): \(2=Ae^0=A\). Therefore \(y=2e^{4x}\).
Equilibrium solutions occur when \(dy/dt=0\). Set \(y(3-y)=0\). This gives \(y=0\) or \(3-y=0\), so \(y=3\). Therefore the equilibrium solutions are the constant solutions \(y(t)=0\) and \(y(t)=3\).
